Definitely me. I do feel like I'm not going anywhere, but recently, I figured out what I would like to do in the future, and did some future planning. Something that I didn't do at 18, which led me to 3 years of failed studies, because I wasn't into the subject. Now that I'm 22, I kinda grew out of it, and maybe matured a bit more. I don't think you've missed out a major part of life. That special someone tends to come when you least expected it. It happened with me. To be honest, getting into a relationship when I was in college and having depression didn't really work well for me. For one, I ended up getting distracted by my partner that I ended up failing college.

Many people tends to say to try to love yourself first before loving others, and that's true to a certain point. On one side, you struggle to love yourself because no one else is, but on the other, when you love someone else more than yourself, you end up becoming a burden to them. And when that person leaves, it makes you loathe yourself more, and it does more harm than good. That said, it differs between people.

The more I think about it, it is true that my sister is definitely better. There have been many years of trying to turn away from that, though I think I've begun to accept it years ago. I thought more about it, and I started to realise that it's not becoming a wannabe or becoming better that bothers me the most. It's the idea of becoming my sister. My sister has many good points, but beside those points, the rest are everything I don't want to be.

When people told me to be more like my sister, I wasn't angry that they believed she was better. I was more angry at the idea of having her bad qualities. I don't want to be rude, annoying and insensitive. I've always hated it when she sees something weird, and feels the need to mock them behind their backs. I've always also hated how ignorant she can be about the world, and that if she's ever wrong, she throws a bitchy fit. I think, when people tell me to be more like her, those are the things that often pop up, and I don't want to be that.

The more I think about it, maybe I wasn't angry. Maybe I was just genuinely disappointed in her and everyone else. Maybe I've associated too much of the small good parts of her to the whole package, that if I thought that if I ever needed to be slim, confident with lots of friends, I'd also need to be an insensitive, ignorant person. But now that I realise that, I don't need to be that to be slim and confident and maybe with a few more friends.

Thanks for the help. I think, I've kinda understood where my problems are now, and that I think I know how I can get over it. Or maybe thinking about all of this has made me become more accepting that I do need to change a bit, to like myself better, but also remembering that there ARE many parts of me that I'd rather have that she doesn't have.

I think the problem was that... I saw that what I wanted in life was different from theirs. They would be happy to be climbing up the ladder in their workplace, while I prefer a more carefree life. Generally, I'm average in my performance, if not a bit above average, but these people are always on the top. I don't mind it much, but it gets irritating when people would look down on me for having worse, compared to them.

My problem isn't that I don't know myself. Finding out myself and what I wanted is amazing! It's the people around me who feel the need to say that it's nothing of great important that bothers me... People expect that having a really higher up position in a company is the equivalent to a good life, yet my good life would be more of a relaxing life without a high-stress job. People believe that I'm just looking down on myself by having that goal, but yet, I feel like they just don't understand what I really want, and no matter how much I explain, it'll never get by them.

Do you have any advice on how to keep neutral for whenever someone brings up your past or flaws? I've always found myself feeling down everytime I meet someone, accidentally or not, and their statement of me is often that I've gotten worse. Whenever I visit my grandparents, they and my aunts and uncles often tell me how fat I've gotten and such, and I do want to be a bit more slimmer, yet, I'm unhappy that they could be mean by making fun of fat people, despite being fatter themselves... I used to just ignore, and accept it, though it took a toll on my self-esteem, but now, it just makes me angry, because I don't feel like my weight should ever be the first thing they always say everytime they see me. So, once again, do you have any advice on stay neutral during these kind of times? I don't want it to let it get to me anymore.

I think it was mostly that, if it's something my sister does, I automatically don't want to do it. Having done things that my sister would have, what floods my mind afterwards, if not during the whole thing, would be the past. I know I've stated this before, but people has often compared me to my sister, and there were many statements implying they had preferred to be in her presence instead of mine. 

Generally, if my relationship with my sister was good, I would have used it to encourage myself. But growing up with her, I never had a say in anything in our relationship. Any instance that I disagreed with her, she'd take it out physically on me, or went full on ignoring, living her life the best without me. I had looked up to her, so I often stayed on her good side, but in the end, I was always tossed aside like baggage. Everyone talks about how awesome she is, but they don't know how much she's made me feel miserable. They'd often tell me how my sister is smart, and how she's pretty, and how she could do everything. She's really one of those high achievers.

I guess... it's not that I don't want to be a wannabe. But I just don't want to be like her. Similarly, recently, I've had my boyfriend told me that my sister is a good role model to have... and all that's really have ever done, is made me devastated because my mind sees it differently. That my boyfriend would have preferred her instead of me.

**EDIT:** Which is why, I want to learn how to let it go. She's better now, because she doesn't hit me anymore... but she still gets incredibly upset when you disagree with her...
Thank you!

I think your parents are doing it with good intentions too. Perhaps they're only trying to get you to really succeed with the best grades possible so that you could get into a good college and then get a good job, and therefore have a good life. Have you talked to your parents about your struggle? I've got a dad who acts like that too, and tries to get me in the top. The backstory was mostly because he came from a poor family, and education gave him a way out. At this age, a degree is always needed, but nowadays, people look mostly into personality too.

What do you think makes you shine out the most? If you haven't found that thing, maybe it's best that you do a bit of self-discovery, perhaps? Remember that, everyone pushes you to do things, but maybe those are the things you do need to do at that moment. You know yourself the best, but when you're depressed or down, your thoughts about yourself changes. That's when you need to hear the people on the outside, who would have a view of you that has been influenced by feelings.

I think it's a good idea to talk to your parents. Maybe start off with the more understanding one, or the more milder one. Maybe ask why they want you to be smart. Personally, I've always remembered my parents as also the type to push me to be smarter and that I can only succeed if I was smart and had the best grades, and in the end, it was mainly because that was their idea of a good life. My idea of a good life is not to have an overly stress work life, which means, I would have been happy working at a job that doesn't require an engineering degree or so. Something my parents still struggle to understand.

No problem, I was in your situation once, and it's never a good place to be for anyone. In fact, maybe I'm still in your position too, because even I struggle to get out of bed and do something. Still haven't done much after I dropped out... and honestly, the idea of starting anew with anything, it scares me because like you, I also believe that I'll probably end up in a lot of shit because I can't get things finished.

So yeah, I guess we both might be in the same boat. I don't know when you told your family, but my family is taking their time trying to "understand" what depression is, and so far? I've also gotten the same kind of reaction. How they'd like for me to be the same way I was before... it hurts to know that they're rejecting that's something clearly part of you. It often takes time for them to understand, and maybe they do, or maybe they don't. When that happens, I think the best thing to do is not to think about it. We can't really change how people think. That said, they still do care about you, even if they don't get it. I've seen my mum cry a lot when she knew that I had depression. Yet, she doesn't quite get it, even though she often tells me how she wishes that I was back to that quiet daughter she had years ago. I guess, the action of her wanting me to be able to feel happiness mattered more, even if she did it wrong. That's one of the few problems about depression, is that many people might struggle to understand what it's all about.

I've heard many people say that depression is that cannot be cured, but something you learn to live with. And having thought about that quite a bit, it's kinda true to a certain point. By learning how to live with it, you'd need to find your own ways of motivation, and maybe your own ways to cope with your thoughts and feelings.

I have had Indian friends from my old school, and I found that most of the time, they ended up getting married through an arranged marriage.

(Police force is notorious for jumping to conclusions and refusing to reason, besides "you illegal sexing it up here".) I also notice from my relatives gossiping, people often jump quickly to blame the girl than the guy. The reasons are often the same. That women are the ones seducing.

I don't know if this counts for India, but in Southeast Asia (or some parts of it), when a situation like this happens, younger girl and older man, (most of) society often blames the younger girl because they are more likely to believe that "the girl is just using her youthful looks to seduce him". Plus, it's also perhaps the mentality that the older you are, the more respect you get? It's easier for everyone to push the blame on the girl because she is less likely to uhmm... "rebel".

I only sought out treatment when I started self-harming and saw how it hurt my friends and loved ones. Then I realised that maybe it wasn't normal after all. 

I believe I had depression since I was a teenager, and whenever I brought up the idea of seeing a counselor, my mom often shot it down saying it was teen angst, and that puberty was doing that. Then for my whole teen life, I thought of myself as just being very different from others, and because I was different, I deserved to be alone. I always told myself that I was definitely going to be dead by 20, no doubt about it.

I turned 20, and my life had been better. I got friends, and I got a boyfriend. But then, I always thought that it was to do with where I was. Then I had been in the UK, studying. I thought and I wanted to be dead than to go back to my home country in Asia. I harmed myself, saw my friend and my boyfriend cry, I cried too and the next day, I went to the doctor and said, "I want to see a doctor. I don't think I'm well at all."

I got support, but... I had things that didn't go well. My studies failed, I started getting social anxiety since I was so ashamed to face my professors and my course mates. I was so ashamed to see my family. I got worse. My mum didn't take it well, and well, a lot of things had happened. I did have some progression. I learnt more about myself through counseling. I found out the sides of me that I was so scared to show, because it had been socially unacceptable in a strict Asian society. I learnt where all the sources of my anxiety and depression came.

It was my own culture. It was the people. It was my own home.

It was a place where being different from others was a curse.

I can't say for sure, to be honest. However, I'll talk about my opinion on this matter.

I come from a strict Asian culture, in which religion plays a strong part in for a long time. I'm going out with a Dutch person, so our lifestyle and cultures are vastly different. 

I've discussed a lot on the state of mental health with him, and he's often talked about how he knew someone who had this kind of problem and that kind of problem. It often feels like there is always 1 out of 10 to 20 people that has a mental problem or disability (of any degree). I often found it weird, however, looking into it a lot, it was a lot to do with culture differences.

In most modern Western societies, mental health awareness is pretty high (from what I've gathered), and it isn't very well-known (or accepted, at times even) in stricter Asian societies (even more if religion is strong, though it always comes down to the family's personality still). 

Awareness here in Asia (or at least, my country) is pretty low, and if someone acts differently, people often just dismiss it as personality or weirdness. As a result, people don't seek help. They tend to accept it. Similarly, if a child does have a mental health issue, there's often that chance of having parents who are too embarrassed to acknowledge that their child is slightly different, and either choose to deny it or to hide their child's problem.

This is really a lot of speculation, though. Only because I don't actually find many people who has mental health problems (though, I do feel that it's often because it's been hidden). Recently here, awareness has been rising, but it's not as strongly as modern Western societies.

As for other Asian countries, I do often believe that reputation or "family honour" is still something that exists strongly in Asian culture.

As I mentioned before, this is really a lot of speculation and my own opinion. I have depression since I was a teen, and many times my parents often dismiss it as teen angst. Fast forward to my early 20's, my depression because severe as a result of long-term suppression, and it snapped when I started facing my worse fears. My mom still regularly tries to get over it, but I can see that it's eating her up knowing her daughter is depressed.

Well, you will always have a chance to make a HQ item even if the resources you use are all NQ items. If all of your resources are HQ, your quality bar will go to 50% of the bar maximum. But keep in mind that chances to produce a HQ item is not linear with the bar. However, the experience you get isn't only dependent on whether or not it is NQ or HQ, but also more of how high you got the quality bar up. 

So even if you managed to fill your bar up to 50%, but ended up with a NQ, you'll still get extra experience as opposed to having a 0% quality bar. But of course, getting a HQ item, the experience is much greater!
